body: ## Expected Behavior A schedule launches workflows as defined in ScheduleIntervalSpec when its offset contains microseconds. ## Actual Behavior A schedule launches only one workflow as defined in ScheduleIntervalSpec when its offset contains microseconds. ## Steps to Reproduce the Problem Define ScheduleIntervalSpec with an offset containing microseconds and send a schedule. Python SDK: ``` temporal_client = await client.Client.connect(TEMPORAL_ADDRESS) interval = timedelta(seconds=120) offset = timedelta(seconds=63, microseconds=123) schedule_spec = ScheduleSpec( intervals=[ScheduleIntervalSpec(every=interval, offset=offset)], ) schedule = Schedule( action=ScheduleActionStartWorkflow("workflow name", None), spec=schedule_spec, ) await temporal_client.create_schedule("bug-repro-schedule", schedule) ``` The first schedule has an offset with microseconds, and the workflow is only launched once (the upcoming runs should have already passed). The second schedule doesn't have microseconds in its offset, and the workflow is launched according to the specified interval and offset. ## Specifications - Version: temporalio==1.18.2 (UI 2.25.0) - Platform: Debian

comments.body:
@dsyurchenko96 What’s your overlap policy? Was the Scheduled Action complete when the next run should have fired?
https://docs.temporal.io/schedule#overlap-policy

The single-launch-on-microsecond-offset pattern points to truncation rather than schedule-state corruption — somewhere on the validation/persistence path the offset is being downcast to second-resolution before the interval calculator sees it, so the next-fire timestamp computed against the truncated offset matches the first fire only by chance (or never matches subsequent intervals at all).

Worth checking which side does the rounding: if the Python SDK serializes the full microsecond value over wire, then the server's offset parser is the culprit; if the SDK already truncates before transport, the issue is client-side. The minimum repro that disambiguates is sending the same workflow definition via two different SDKs (Python + Go) — if both fail identically, server-side; if only one fails, SDK-side.

Either way, the fix surface for either layer should also add an explicit-precision contract — `ScheduleIntervalSpec.offset` documenting which resolutions are supported (and either rejecting sub-second offsets loudly or supporting them end-to-end). Silent truncation of user-provided durations is the failure class.

title: Schedule with microseconds in offset launches only once
